options: Because it's the basis that quantum hardware is physically built to use when reporting measurement outcomes, and the one circuit diagrams and results default to
Because it's the only mathematically valid basis for a qubit
Because it was the first basis discovered historically, before any alternatives existed
Because computers can only perform arithmetic using 0 and 1, so quantum states must match
questions.explain: The computational basis gets its name because it matches what the hardware's measurement actually reports -- it's a convention tied to readout, not a deeper mathematical necessity.

questions.q: Are |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 a valid orthonormal basis for a single qubit?
options: Yes -- both are normalized ((1/√2)²+(1/√2)²=1 each, verified) and they are mutually orthogonal, so {|+⟩,|−⟩} is just as valid a basis as {|0⟩,|1⟩}
No -- only {|0⟩,|1⟩} can ever be used as a measurement basis
Yes, but only because |+⟩ and |−⟩ happen to equal |0⟩ and |1⟩
No -- |+⟩ and |−⟩ are not normalized
questions.explain: Both |+⟩ and |−⟩ satisfy the normalization condition (verified: (1/√2)²+(1/√2)²=1) and are orthogonal to each other, so together they form a perfectly legitimate orthonormal basis -- just a different one from the computational basis.

questions.q: What does it mean, mathematically, to express |0⟩ as (|+⟩+|−⟩)/√2?
options: It's the same physical state |0⟩, rewritten in terms of a different orthonormal basis -- a change of coordinates, not a change to the state itself
It means |0⟩ is secretly a 50/50 mixture of two different particles
It means |0⟩ no longer satisfies normalization
It means the computational basis has been replaced permanently
questions.explain: Any state in this 2D space can be written in either basis -- it's a change of coordinates, exactly like re-expressing an ordinary vector in a rotated coordinate frame. The physical state |0⟩ doesn't change at all.

questions.q: Why is the statement 'the qubit's state is 0 or 1' considered incomplete without specifying a basis?
options: Because a state that looks definite in the computational basis can look like an even split when measured in a different basis, such as the X-basis
Because 0 and 1 are not valid quantum states at all
Because a qubit can never actually be in state |0⟩ or |1⟩
Because the computational basis doesn't actually exist in real hardware
questions.explain: Which outcome 'definite' refers to depends entirely on which basis you measure in. A computational-basis-definite state like |0⟩ is an equal superposition when measured in the X-basis, so basis matters to the meaning of the claim.

questions.q: Why do quantum algorithms often rotate a qubit's state into a different basis mid-circuit and then rotate it back before the final measurement?
options: To set up interference effects correctly in the alternate basis, then return to the computational basis because that's the basis the hardware actually reads out at the end
Because quantum hardware cannot physically apply gates in the computational basis
Because the computational basis becomes invalid after the first gate is applied
Purely for cosmetic/visual reasons in circuit diagrams, with no computational effect
questions.explain: Basis rotations (e.g. via Hadamard) are a deliberate algorithmic tool for arranging interference, and circuits rotate back to the computational basis before measurement because that's the basis real hardware reports results in.
